short: The first comprehensive English-language liturgy was mandated for all church services.
full:
Introduced on 9 June 1549 through the Act of Uniformity, the Book of Common Prayer officially replaced the various Latin liturgical rites previously used throughout England. Chiefly authored and compiled by Archbishop Thomas Cranmer during the strongly Protestant reign of Edward VI, it provided a single, standardized English liturgy for daily morning and evening prayer, Sundays, and all holy sacraments.

The book served as a profound cornerstone of the English Reformation, radically reshaping how ordinary people experienced Sunday worship. While the initial 1549 edition offered a carefully moderate theological compromise, it still violently sparked the Prayer Book Rebellion in the conservative West Country. Later, significantly more Protestant revisions formed the bedrock of the global Anglican tradition that persists today.
